questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to learn Latin and ancient Greek at school
How much of modern English still comes from Old English
The history of the Vikings and their battles in Britain
Why English spelling is so difficult for foreign learners
questions.why: They discuss Old English and how much of the English we use today comes from it.

questions.q: What was Neil saying at the start of the programme?
options: 'Good morning' in Old English
A line from an old poem he had learned
A greeting in modern French
'Goodbye' in Latin
questions.why: He says he was saying 'Good morning, pleased to meet you' in Anglo-Saxon, or Old English.

questions.q: What kind of words have survived from Old English, according to Neil's list?
options: Mostly scientific and medical words
Words about law and government
Words for technology
Basic everyday words
questions.why: He lists words like beer, bread, eye, hand, mother and brother – all Anglo-Saxon.

questions.q: According to Neil, what is the history of English closely linked to?
options: Trade with China
The work of famous poets
Invasions by other peoples
The spread of printing
questions.why: Neil says 'the history of English is the history of invasions'.

questions.q: What point does Professor Andy Orchard make with the example 'I texted'?
options: Young people are changing English with new technology
Even new verbs use the Old English '-ed' ending
'Text' is actually a very old Old English word
Modern English no longer has any real grammar rules
questions.why: He says 'text' comes from Latin, but with 'texted' and 'tweeted' 'we still lapse to the Anglo-Saxon'.

questions.q: About how much of everyday spoken English comes from Old English, according to the discussion?
options: About 20%
About half
Almost none
Around 80%
questions.why: Rosen suggests about 80% in common parlance, and Orchard says in speech it would be something like that.

questions.q: What joke does Professor Orchard make about Old English poetry?
options: It is always about food, feasts and drinking
Nobody today can read or understand it at all
It is always raining, just like today
It was all written by Vikings in the north
questions.why: He says 'in Old English poetry it's always raining and I suppose it's always raining today'.

questions.q: What is Professor Orchard's final conclusion about modern English?
options: Despite invasions and empire, it is still Old English
It is now mostly French because of the Norman invasion
It has completely lost its connection with the past
It is now closer to Latin than it is to Old English
questions.why: He says despite the invasions and empire, today's English is still 'at its heart' Old English.
